topic: Ultrafast LLM tiers and latency SLOs
angle: Speed changes product behavior more than small quality gains; design your routing and SLOs around latency first.
sourceTitle: Previewing Ultrafast mode: GPT-5.6 Sol at up to 14X the speed
linkedinPost:
Speed changes user behavior more than small quality gains. Ultrafast LLM tiers make that painfully obvious. ⏱️

OpenAI just previewed a GPT‑5.6 “Ultrafast” tier hitting up to 750 tok/s and ~14x speedups. That’s not a brag number; it’s a product constraint shift. When latency drops, users escalate less, accept more automation, and expect instant follow‑ups.

In FDE work, the biggest wins came from treating latency like a budget. Example: we split chat flows into three routes—“burst lane” (fast/simple intent), “steady lane” (reasoned + tools), and “human lane” (handoff). The fast path got cheaper models, low temperature, aggressive timeouts, and streaming partials; the heavy path got tool-use and eval gating.

Two concrete tips:
- Hedge requests with timeouts and fallbacks; let the fast answer win.
- Build circuit breakers around RAG and functions—slow knowledge calls ruin your SLOs more than model decode ever will.

A recent OpenAI post frames this as smarter model selection and a new Responses API. My take: start with a latency SLO, then design routing, evals, and backpressure to hit it. Quality improvements matter—but not if they arrive 2s late.

How are you budgeting latency across your LLM stack today? #AIEngineering #LLM #FDE #ForwardDeployedEngineer
